title: Real-Time Analytics
description: Design and build end-to-end real-time analytics pipelines using Kafka Streams and supporting infrastructure.

data.text: **Real-time analytics** transforms raw event streams into live metrics, dashboards, and alerts. A typical pipeline ingests events into Kafka, applies stream processing to filter, transform, and aggregate data, stores results in a queryable analytics store, and surfaces insights through visualization tools. Because the pipeline operates on data as it arrives, stakeholders can detect anomalies, track KPIs, and respond to incidents within seconds rather than hours.

A real-time analytics pipeline has five logical stages: **ingestion** (Kafka producers write events to topics), **processing** (Kafka Streams or ksqlDB applies business logic), **storage** (aggregated results are written to ClickHouse, Druid, or a relational database), **visualization** (Grafana or Superset renders live dashboards), and **alerting** (anomaly detectors or threshold rules trigger notifications). Each stage can scale independently.

terms.definition: Analyzing data as it is produced, with latency measured in seconds or sub-seconds.
Online Analytical Processing — querying aggregated data across dimensions for reporting and dashboards.
Identifying unusual patterns in real-time data using statistical thresholds or machine learning.
Guaranteeing that each event affects downstream metrics exactly once, even after failures.

data.text: The processing stage applies several common patterns. **Filtering** removes noise by discarding irrelevant events (for example, health-check pings). **Transformation** normalizes fields, enriches with reference data, or converts units. **Aggregation** computes counts, sums, averages, percentiles, or distinct counts over windows. **CEP (Complex Event Processing)** detects sequences of events that match a pattern, such as a user logging in and then abandoning a cart within five minutes.

data.text: After processing, results must be stored in a system optimized for low-latency analytical queries. **ClickHouse** excels at column-oriented aggregations over time-series data. **Apache Druid** is purpose-built for real-time OLAP with sub-second query response. **TimescaleDB** extends PostgreSQL with hypertables for time-series workloads. Visualization tools such as **Grafana** connect directly to these stores and refresh dashboards on a configurable interval, often every one to five seconds.

data.title: End-to-End Exactly-Once
data.text: To achieve end-to-end exactly-once semantics, enable idempotent Kafka producers, transactional writes from the stream processor, and idempotent consumers in the analytics store. This prevents duplicate metrics even if the processor restarts mid-window.

items.question: What latency can I expect from end to end?
items.answer: With Kafka Streams and ClickHouse, end-to-end latency is typically 1-5 seconds for aggregation results to appear in Grafana. Network and dashboard refresh intervals add variability.

items.question: How do I handle late-arriving events in analytics?
items.answer: Use windowed aggregations with grace periods, and configure the analytics store to update existing records. ClickHouse supports UPDATE and projection tables for late corrections.

items.question: Should I use Kafka Streams or a dedicated stream processor like Flink?
items.answer: Use Kafka Streams for simpler pipelines that fit within a JVM service. Use Flink when you need advanced features such as complex event processing, large-scale state, or exactly-once across multiple sinks.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Real-time analytics pipelines ingest, process, store, and visualize events with sub-minute latency
Use windowed aggregations to compute metrics over unbounded streams
Choose storage based on query patterns: columnar OLAP for dashboards, time-series for metrics
End-to-end exactly-once requires cooperation between producer, processor, and consumer
data.takeaway: Real-time analytics turns event streams into a competitive advantage by delivering live visibility into business and system health.

data.title: Exercise: Design a Real-Time Dashboard
data.description: Design a real-time analytics pipeline that tracks website page views and error rates, then visualizes them in a live dashboard.
steps: Identify the event sources: web servers emitting page_view and error events
Define the Kafka topics and partitioning strategy
Design the Kafka Streams topology: filter noise, enrich with country data, aggregate per-minute counts
Choose an analytics store and define the schema for storing metrics
Sketch the Grafana dashboard layout and specify which panels show page views, error rate, and top pages
data.expectedOutcome: A pipeline architecture document covering topics, processing logic, storage schema, and dashboard design
